lines: Chat has just remembered an earlier moment.
The engine finds the original clip, checks the connection, and brings it back onto the stream.
The date and the reason appear with it.
Streamers can have years of clips, but nobody can search that history while producing a live show.
Callbacks are some of the best moments on stream.
They depend on remembering the right thing at the right time.
I connect my channel and explicitly index my own clips.
The index uses real clip titles, categories, dates, and thumbnails from the API.
Embeddings let the engine compare a rolling chat window with those memories.
The activity graph shows messages actually received.
The candidate feed explains the connection and shows competing matches.
Community mode needs three voices. This recording uses a labeled rehearsal with my own live messages.
Here, the engine holds a near miss instead of forcing a callback.
A qualifying automatic callback gives me seven seconds to veto it.
Cooldown and duplicate checks protect the timing. When it airs, the bot posts the original clip link.
I built this in one Codex thread, starting with the experience I wanted for streamers and chat.
Codex implemented the Helix clip index, server-side authorization, and EventSub chat connection.
It built semantic retrieval, the airing gates, and the synchronized overlay.
In this thread, we tested account isolation, veto cancellation, rate limits, and overlay delivery.
We also checked phone layouts, both themes, and transparency in a real browser source.
All demo clips come from my own channel.
The public replay needs no account, so anyone can try the same interaction.
Callback gives a community's shared history a way back into the conversation.
